sweep_summary: Diriku-Shambyu (Gciriku/Rumanyo, Bantu K.332) is not in the catalog. Both Glottolog stress-title items are by Möhlig and are about this language's word prosody. Möhlig 1969 (ZDMG Suppl. I, held by the project from the ULB Halle scan) was read in full: it summarises his 1967 thesis and states that Dciriku distinguishes unstressed, weakly and strongly stressed syllables, that stress bundles with tone and length into 10 combination classes, and that the language has 2 lexically distinctive prosodemes (plus 3 ordinative, 2+ expressive) — i.e. stress is lexically/morphologically distributed, with no fixed positional word stress (Möhlig 1981 calls the type 'interval-accent'). Möhlig 1967 (the 321-p. Köln dissertation, prosodology pp. 63-109, stress pp. 66-100 per Fodor 1977) remains print only (no HathiTrust/KUPS/archive.org copy; Google Books blocked this search of works with stress in the title). Additional sources found: Sommer 2003:571 (read; Gciriku prosodeme minimal pair with 'respiratory stress', citing Möhlig 1997:220), Fodor 1977:68-69 (read; secondhand 'several types of main and secondary stress'), Möhlig 1981 (snippets), Möhlig 1997 dialectometry chapter (print), Möhlig 2005 sketch and Möhlig & Shiyaka-Mberema 2005 dictionary (paid Köppe PDFs; highest acquisition priority for a modern English statement), Westphal 1970 review (first page only). Lusakalalu 2003 (open, downloaded) is silent on stress.

new_statements.translation: As regards intensity (stress) classes, Dciriku distinguishes unaccented syllabics, strongly accented and weakly accented syllabics. [...] the prosodic classes [tone, stress, length] always occur in combination. [...] Instead of the 24 possible combinations only 10 combination classes are found in Dciriku. This restriction suggests [...] that linguistic relevance belongs to the prosodic combination classes and not to the simple prosodic classes. [...] For Dciriku the procedure finally yields two distinctive prosodemes (DP), three ordinative prosodemes (OP) and at least two expressive prosodemes (EP). [...] DP I = class (1) [high tone, strong stress, short] ... (5) on monosyllabic stems ...; DP II = 3←(8) [falling, strong stress, long] on polysyllabic stems [...] Rising and falling tones are always strongly stressed.

Juli 1968 in Würzburg: Vorträge, Teil 3 (Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Supplementa I,3), 1155-1165. Wiesbaden: Franz Steiner.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Möhlig does not describe an independent word stress with a fixed position. Stress (Druckakzent: strong/weak/none) is one component of tone-stress-length bundles ('prosodemes'); the two lexically distinctive prosodemes (DP I = high+strong stress+short, realised over the bearer syllable and the following one; DP II = falling+strong stress+long, or high spread over the stem) are carried by stem syllables (monosyllabic vs polysyllabic stems), so strong stress co-occurs with the high element of the lexical tone interval on the stem rather than falling on a counted syllable of the word. Contour (rising/falling) tones are always strongly stressed. In his 1981 typology Möhlig calls Dciriku an 'interval-accent language' (Druckakzent-Intervall-Sprache) rather than a true tone language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A weak stress grade (schwacher Druckakzent) is distinguished from strong stress; e.g. combination class (2) high+weak+short and (5) low+weak+short; class (5) is a positional variant of DP I on monosyllabic stems. No rhythmic secondary-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: In emphatic environment combination class (6) (low, accentless? / positional variant) neutralises the DP I vs DP II contrast; expressive prosodeme EP II (classes 1+12) falls on the last syllable of a word or morpheme complex; prosodemes are 'sequential', spreading onto neighbouring syllables across morpheme boundaries, and monosyllabic stems/formatives perturb neighbouring syllables; elicited single words come out as enumerative/deictic/one-word-sentence forms with markedly different prosodic shapes (p. 1156).
new_statements.domain_note: Analysis is explicitly of connected free speech (tape-recorded narrative), not citation forms; Möhlig warns that isolated words in Dciriku/Kwangali/Herero yield deviating prosodic shapes. Distinctive prosodemes are properties of stems/monemes (lexical-morphological domain); ordinative prosodemes mark phrase/sentence/word grouping; expressive ones mark question, command, emphasis.
new_statements.identity_note: All Möhlig sources describe the Gciriku (his spelling 'Dciriku', later 'Rugciriku', Guthrie K332 / K38b) dialect of Rumanyo, from 1960s fieldwork on the middle Kavango (Namibia); the other dialect, Shambyu (Rushambyu), is not separately described. Glottolog diri1252 'Diriku-Shambyu' [diu] covers both.

new_statements.quote: An Schalldruckklassen müssen im Dciriku unterschieden werden akzentlose silbentragende Laute stark akzentuierte und schwach akzentuierte silbentragende Laute So wenig wie in den Tonhöhenklassen die absolute Tonhöhe relevant ist so wenig hängen auch die Druckakzente von der absolut feststellbaren Druckstärke eines silbentragenden Lautes ab [p. 1158] ... Im Dciriku ergeben sich am Ende des Verfahrens zwei distinktive Prosodeme kurz DP drei ordinative Prosodeme kurz OP und wenigstens zwei expressive Prosodeme kurz EP [p. 1162] (scanned text, punctuation lost)
new_statements.translation: As stress classes, Dciriku must distinguish unstressed syllable-bearing sounds, strongly stressed and weakly stressed syllable-bearing sounds. Just as absolute pitch is irrelevant in the tone classes, the stresses do not depend on the absolutely measurable intensity of a syllable-bearing sound. ... In Dciriku the procedure yields in the end two distinctive prosodemes (DP), three ordinative prosodemes (OP) and at least two expressive prosodemes (EP).
new_statements.citation: Möhlig, Wilhelm Johann Georg (1969). Zur prosodologischen Analyse sogenannter Tonsprachen im Bantu. In W. Voigt (ed.), XVII. Deutscher Orientalistentag.. Würzburg: Vorträge (ZDMG Supplementa I), 1155-1165. Wiesbaden: Steiner.
new_statements.reading: First-hand (author of the only full grammar). Dciriku has a three-degree stress contrast (none / weak / strong) that is not positional: stress combines with tone (H, L, F, R) and length into 10 attested combination classes, and only these bundles carry function. Two lexically distinctive prosodemes result (DP I: high + strong stress + short before a prosodeme-less syllable; DP II: high + unstressed + short, or falling + strong + long, on polysyllabic stems); rising/falling tones are always strongly stressed; an expressive prosodeme (EP II) falls on the last syllable of a word. So there is no fixed word-stress rule (no penult/initial statement); stress is a lexically distributed component of a tone-stress-length 'interval-accent' system. Consistent with Sommer 2003:571 (citing Möhlig 1997:220) and Fodor 1977:69 (citing Möhlig 1967:66-100). Coding suggestion: lexical/prosodeme-based (tone-plus-stress) accent, not fixed stress.

sources.note: Dciriku prosody analysed as 'prosodemes' = fixed bundles of tone, stress (Druckakzent: unaccented / weakly / strongly accented syllables) and length; only 10 of 24 possible tone-stress-length combinations occur, so stress is not an independent system; 2 distinctive prosodemes (DP I high-strong-short, DP II falling-strong-long etc.) sit on stems (monosyllabic/polysyllabic), 3 ordinative and >=2 expressive prosodemes (EP II on the last syllable of a word); rising and falling tones are always strongly stressed. No fixed-position word-stress rule is given.

sources.citation: Sommer, Gabriele (2003). Western Savanna (K, R). In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 566-580. London: Routledge.
sources.quote: 'In Gciriku, for instance, tone intervals seem to interact with other prosodic features such as stress, accent and vowel length as in presentative constructions like şì-dírà "it is a taboo" which contrasts with şí-dîirà "it is a bird". While in the first case the descending interval spreads over two subsequent syllables and the high toned syllable bears an additional respiratory stress and has a short vowel, the second distinctive prosodeme is also marked by a descending interval; in this case it spreads over the first syllable only and is accompanied by lengthening of the respective vowel segment (Möhlig 1997:220).'
sources.note: Second-hand (citing Möhlig 1997:220): whether tone is distinctive in Kavango is debated; 'In Gciriku, for instance, tone intervals seem to interact with other prosodic features such as stress, accent and vowel length', e.g. şì-dírà 'it is a taboo' (descending interval over two syllables, high syllable with additional respiratory stress and short vowel) vs şí-dîirà 'it is a bird' (descending interval on one lengthened syllable). Also: vowel length not phonologically distinctive in Gciriku (Möhlig 1997:218).

sources.quote: p. 69: 'According to Westermann and Ward [1957:113-115], in African languages stress does not exist in the form peculiar to European idioms. But the important role of dynamic accent was evidenced in Dciriku [Möhlig 1967:66-100], where several types of main and secondary stress occur, together with other distinctive components.' p. 68: 'Concerning Dciriku, the author included the quantitative differences of the vowels as a feature in the structure of the distinctive prosodemes--besides tonemes and stress--although no minimal pairs were shown.'
sources.note: Secondhand summary of Möhlig 1967 pp. 66-100: several types of main and secondary stress, functioning together with tone and length as components of distinctive prosodemes. Gives the page range of the stress chapter in the unobtainable thesis.

sources.quote: p. 24: '... dciriku, une syllabe peut porter un des deux prosodèmes distinctifs, symbolisés ici par I ou II.
